k.s: Expands each row's (offset, length) descriptor into index_length explicit KV indices, translating through block_tables when has_block_tables is set. Requires a power-of-two block size so the divide/modulo collapse to a shift and a mask, and tiles the row in B-

Builds all six fixed-stride DFlash draft inputs in one launch — slot mapping, positions, input ids, valid-token mask, gate_force_random and the padded kv_index rows — for real_cnt requests of dflash_block_size tokens each. A request with first_token_position <

nodes.s: Ascend backend of the multimodal image pipeline: three TileLang kernels that splice image/pad embeddings into the token embedding table, turn raw packed RGB bytes into normalized bf16 ViT patches, and pool or transpose-concat d x d windows of ViT patch features.

k.s: Kernel factory: in place overwrites embedding rows of image tokens with images_embeds[offset-1] (inclusive prefix count) and rows of the i-th pad token with image_pad_embeds[i], gathering a [B, hidden] UB tile per vector core.

Kernel factory: converts packed HWC uint8 RGB bytes into normalized bf16 patch tensors, centering each real image inside its n_vit grid and emitting pad_color outside it; reads source pixels straight from global memory because centered rows are not contiguous.
Kernel factory: stages the d x d window of ViT patch features into a UB tile and either mean-pools it to one [dim] row or transposes it into [dim, d, d]; ragged right/bottom blocks are zero-filled.

nodes.s: Ascend kernel that concatenates the sliding-window KV index and the compressed-attention KV index into the two strided halves of one output row, shifting the CA half by total_k_swa + total_k while keeping -1 padding intact.

k.s: Kernel factory: two Persistent passes copy the SWA index verbatim and add the global KV offset to the CA index with a SIMD select that preserves -1 sentinels.

nodes.s: Ascend backend of the context-parallel index preparation: two fused kernels that compute hierarchical prefix sums and then scatter the mirror-CP permutation indices (and the YOCO full-to-compact redistribution indices) in a single device launch.

k.s: Kernel factory: phase 1 builds the per-compress-ratio and mirror-row cumulative lengths, phase 2 scatters mirror_cp_index / mirror_cp_reverse_index and the per-ratio (ks, ke) ranges for this CP rank; the two phases are separated by an inter-core barrier.

Kernel factory: prepares the YOCO full-to-compact CP redistribution indices — per-rank kept-token prefixes, this rank's contribution indices, and the reverse indices into the rank-major all-gather buffer.

nodes.s: Ascend kernels that materialize every per-token decode metadata tensor of the V4 model in one pass — positions, validity and routing masks, context lengths, per-sparse-ratio key lengths, SWA and compressed-attention slot mappings — plus a standalone block-table expansion kernel.

k.s: Kernel factory: expands the compact 1D per-sequence block table into the per-token 2D block_tables_out, replicating each sequence's row across its query tokens.

Kernel factory: for every query token writes position, valid/gate/routing masks, context length, per-sparse-ratio klen, per-dense-ratio CA index offsets, the SWA ring-buffer window and store slot, the query index (placeholders get a sentinel), and per-CA-ratio

nodes.s: Ascend kernel that turns per-sequence MTP confidence rates into variable query lengths: it accumulates each sequence's cumulative acceptance probability per draft step, then globally ranks all candidate draft tokens and keeps those inside the total_q budget.

k.s: Kernel factory: phase 1 writes cum_rates as the running product of the previous step's confidence rates, phase 2 ranks every (sequence, step) candidate against all others and sets seqlens_q to 1 plus the number of its steps that beat the extra-token budget.

nodes.s: Ascend kernels that move the per-layer compression state between the KV-store ring buffer layout and the inference tensor layout, in both directions, as a strided uint8 copy.

k.s: Shared kernel body: one Persistent task per (layer, token) copies feature_dim bytes through UB between state_cache and state_tensor, resolving both ring-buffer positions modulo their own block sizes; direction is fixed by cache_to_tensor.
Public factory for the cache-to-tensor direction: reads the state ring buffer into the inference tensor.
Public factory for the tensor-to-cache direction: writes the inference tensor back into the state ring buffer.

nodes.s: Ascend kernel that scatters per-request MTP outputs — predicted token ids, full-vocabulary logprobs, an optional index tensor and confidence — from the step-local tensors into the persistent pooled MTP info buffers, skipping requests whose write slot is 0.

k.s: Kernel factory: one Persistent task per (request, draft step, vocab chunk) copies the logprob chunk (and index chunk) into the pool rows at slot*nextn+step; the first chunk also writes the token id and confidence.

nodes.s: Ascend kernel for grammar-constrained decoding: applies a packed 32-bit token bitmask to a logits row in place, setting every disallowed vocabulary entry to -inf for one MTP step.

k.s: Kernel factory: resolves each row through indices (and, with has_ftp, through the first-token-position table plus the step offset), then masks the logits tile by tile with SIMD bit tests against the bitmask words.

nodes.s: Ascend kernel that, for each token, sums exp(logprob) over every vocabulary entry ranked below the sampled one — strictly smaller logprobs plus equal ones at a lower index — giving the sampled token's tail probability mass.

k.s: Kernel factory: per token, pipelines the vocab in 8192-element chunks, accumulates predicated exp() sums against the sampled token's logprob pivot, and reduces the accumulator to one scalar on the last chunk; rows with a negative sample index write 0.

nodes.s: Ascend kernel that expands per-row (offset1, len1, offset2, len2) pivots into a dense sliding-window KV index row — the two ring-buffer segments concatenated, with -1 past the window.

k.s: Kernel factory: a SIMD lane-index comparison picks offset1+col for columns inside the first segment, offset2-len1+col for the second, and -1 beyond both, writing width columns per row.

nodes.s: Empty package marker for the CUDA TileLang backend; ops.py enumerates this package's modules with pkgutil and re-exports every *_tl factory it finds.

CUDA kernels for sparse-attention block selection: block-level max pooling of the selector logits with on-device task compaction, the compacted token count per row, and in-place restoration of compact indices back to absolute token indices.

k.s: Kernel factory: a prep kernel computes per-request-group task counts, their prefix sums and the flat task id list, then persistent CTAs max-reduce each block of selector logits into block_scores, forcing the last valid block of every row to +inf so it is alway
Kernel factory: sums the clamped token count of every selected candidate block to give each row's compacted key length.
Kernel factory: maps compact top-k indices back to absolute token indices through the candidate block table (optionally adding a per-row offset), writing -1 for invalid slots.

nodes.s: CUDA kernels for KV compression: a softmax-weighted pooling over a COMPRESS_RATIO window of (score, latent) pairs that also maintains the per-sequence state ring buffer, in separate prefill and decode variants.

k.s: Picks the (DIM_BLOCK, NUM_DIM_BLOCKS, threads) compute tiling: a power-of-two tile dividing dim with at most 4096 elements per compression window.

Kernel factory for prefill: softmax over the scores of each compression window, weighted sum of the latents into kv_compressed, with window tokens read either from the state cache (previous chunk) or from the current score/latent tensors; a second kernel store

Kernel factory for decode: stores every token's (score, latent) into the ring buffer, then, only on tokens that close a compression window, reads the window back and emits the softmax-weighted compressed KV row.

nodes.s: CUDA kernel that fixes up seqlens_k in place across the zero-overhead-scheduling boundary: adds this step's query length and, for sequences carried over from the previous step, subtracts the draft tokens that were rejected.

k.s: Kernel factory: one thread per sequence computes seqlens_k += seqlens_q and, when remap points at a previous-step entry, corrects it by prev_num_accepted_tokens - nextn.

nodes.s: CUDA kernel that fills the DFlash graph's per-request input tensors: the first src_req_cnt rows from the real request tensors and the remaining rows from the padding tensors, so the captured graph always sees a fixed request count.

k.s: Kernel factory: one thread per destination request copies positions, sampling parameters, seeds and MTP write slots from either the source or the padding tensors.

nodes.s: CUDA kernels of the DFlash draft path: a fused confidence head (bf16 GEMV over the hidden state plus an optional Markov embedding, temperature-scaled sigmoid) and the hidden-state store that averages the hc_mult copies into the DFlash input buffer.

k.s: Kernel factory: one CTA per token runs a pipelined bf16 GEMV against the shared confidence weight (hidden part, then the Markov-rank part when present) and writes sigmoid(sum/temp) clamped to +/-60.
Kernel factory: copies x[token, 0] into the strided DFlash input row when hc_mult is 1, otherwise averages the hc_mult hidden copies in fp32 before storing.

nodes.s: CUDA kernel that rewrites FlashMLA's per-token top-k KV indices in place from logical positions into physical paged-cache slots, masking everything beyond context_lens with -1.

k.s: Kernel factory: one CTA per (batch, query) maps each top-k index through block_tables into block*block_size + offset, writing -1 past the context length.

nodes.s: CUDA kernel that builds the per-token n-gram id windows feeding the Engram embedding lookup, stitching across the zero-overhead-scheduling boundary: carried-over requests take their recent ids from the previous step's sampled and predicted tokens, fresh ones from the current batch.

k.s: Kernel factory: for every query token walks the max_ngram_size history backwards, taking ids from the compressed window, the previous step's sampled/predicted ids (mapped through lookup_table) or the fresh tokens, and pads after an image sentinel.

nodes.s: CUDA kernel that assembles the step's flat input_ids: for requests carried over from the previous step the first slot takes the previously sampled token and the rest the previously predicted draft tokens, otherwise the freshly scheduled tokens are used.

k.s: Kernel factory: one CTA per sequence writes seqlens_q tokens at the cu_seqlens_q offset, choosing between prev_sampled_token_ids / prev_predict_token_ids and fresh_tokens by the remap entry.

nodes.s: CUDA kernel for a generic row gather Y = X[index] over a strided source, zero-filling rows whose index is out of range; tile width, register buffer size and block count are chosen from the feature dimension.

k.s: Kernel factory: picks the (BD, BM) tiling from D, then each CTA loads its index slice and copies the corresponding rows of X into Y, substituting zeros for negative or out-of-bounds indices.

nodes.s: CUDA backend of the multimodal image pipeline: splices image and pad embeddings into the token embedding table, converts packed HWC uint8 RGB bytes into normalized bf16 ViT patches, and pools or transpose-concats d x d windows of ViT patch features.

k.s: Kernel factory: one CTA per token overwrites the embedding row with images_embeds[offset-1] for the image token id, or with image_pad_embeds[i] when the token matches the i-th pad id.
Kernel factory: one CTA per output patch center-pads each real image into its n_vit grid, fills the border with the quantized pad color, and normalizes into the bf16 patch tensor.

Kernel factory: one CTA per output patch gathers the d x d window of ViT features (zero-filling ragged edges) and either mean-pools it in fp32 into one [dim] row or transpose-concats it into [dim, d, d].

nodes.s: CUDA counterpart of the KV index concatenation: copies the sliding-window index and the compressed-attention index into the two strided halves of one output row, offsetting the CA half by total_k_swa + total_k and keeping -1 padding.

k.s: Kernel factory: derives the per-CTA row count, register budget and pipeline depth from the two widths, then streams both index halves through fragments, adding the global KV offset to non-sentinel CA entries.

nodes.s: CUDA debug kernel that scans a flattened tensor for NaN or values at or beyond max_abs, prints the offending id, value and offset, and fires a device assertion.

k.s: Kernel factory: each thread checks its elements in fp32 and calls printf plus T.device_assert(False) on the first NaN or out-of-range value.

nodes.s: CUDA backend of the context-parallel index preparation: two kernels that fuse the per-sequence prefix scan with an output-parallel scatter, producing the mirror-CP permutation and its reverse, the per-compress-ratio key ranges, and the YOCO full-to-compact redistribution indices.

k.s: Kernel factory: a prefix kernel builds cu_lens for the mirror rows and each compress ratio, then an output-parallel kernel writes mirror_cp_reverse_index, mirror_cp_index (-1 for padding) and the per-ratio (ks, ke) key ranges for this CP rank.
Kernel factory: builds the YOCO full-to-compact CP boundary indices — per-rank kept-token prefixes, this rank's contribution index list and the reverse index into the rank-major all-gather buffer.

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang backend for V4.1 decode metadata preparation: one 128-thread block per sequence fills seventeen per-token output tensors in a single launch — positions, validity and routing masks, context lengths, SWA ring-buffer offsets and store slots, query indices, state-block ids, plus per-compression-ratio klen, compressed positions and compressed-KV store slots. A second factory expands the compact 1-D block table into the per-token 2-D form. Pure index arithmetic, memory-bound, DeepSeek-original execution-plane code with no vLLM lineage.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory for the fused decode-metadata kernel. Window size, block sizes, the load-balance override and the three compression-ratio tuples are compile-time constants; the returned prim_func writes positions, masks, context lengths, SWA offsets and s

Companion factory expanding the compact 1-D block table plus its per-sequence offsets into the dense per-token 2-D `block_tables_out`. Chunked over a 1,024-entry BLOCK_SIZE purely to keep the register-count estimate from overflowing.

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang kernel behind variable-length speculative verification: phase one builds the cumulative product of per-draft-token confidence rates (read through a remap table, 0.0 for freshly admitted sequences), phase two ranks every (sequence, draft position) pair globally by that rate and keeps the positions that fall inside the `total_q - num_seqs` extra-token budget, writing each sequence's `1 + accepted` query length. This is the GPU-side recomputation of per-request draft lengths that CPU scheduling cannot know in time under asynchronous scheduling.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory producing the two-phase kernel that turns per-draft-token confidence rates into per-sequence query lengths: cumulative product first, then a sortless global ranking that keeps the highest-rate draft positions fitting inside the step's extr

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang gather/scatter pair moving per-sequence state (SWA) KV between the kvstore circular buffer and the inference-side circular buffer. `select_state_slice_tl` copies cache to tensor one token row per block; `load_state_to_cache_tl` copies tensor to cache treating each layer as a flat byte stream tiled over `threads x gcd(8, feature_dim)` bytes. Both operate on uint8 strided tensors, are purely memory-bound, and arm PDL synchronization only when a layer exceeds 64 KB.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory for the cache-to-tensor gather: copies `block_size_inference` token rows ending at `last_hit_position` out of the kvstore circular buffer into the inference circular buffer, one row per block, with both source and destination indices wrapp

TileLang JIT factory for the tensor-to-cache scatter: treats each layer as a flat byte stream of `block_size_inference * feature_dim` bytes and has each block move `threads * gcd(8, feature_dim)` bytes, recovering token and feature indices by division — a layo

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang kernel that persists one decode step's MTP (multi-token prediction) output into the pooled draft buffers — token ids, per-step confidences and the full vocab-wide logprob row, plus its index row when top-k logprobs were requested. One block per (request, draft step) copies the vocabulary dimension through register fragments in `min(threads*16, next_pow2(vocab))`-wide blocks; a `write_slots[req] == 0` sentinel skips requests that need no record.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory for the MTP record-store kernel. `nextn`, `vocab_size` and the two optional-channel flags are compile-time constants that pick the thread count and fragment width; the kernel writes token ids and confidences once per request (step 0) and t

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang kernel applying a grammar bitmask to logits in place for structured output: each block stages `128*64` logits and the matching 32-bit mask words into shared memory and drives every token whose bit is clear to -inf. With `has_ftp` the logits row is resolved through a first-token-position table plus the step index, so one per-request bitmask can be applied to the correct draft step of a variable-length speculative batch, and blocks past the request's last row return early.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory for the in-place grammar-mask kernel; `has_ftp` selects between indexing logits directly by request and resolving the row through a first-token-position table plus the draft step, which is what makes one bitmask usable across a variable-le

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang reduction summing exp(logprob) over every vocabulary entry ranked at or below the sampled token — the tail probability mass used to score a sample and to drive speculative rejection. One block per token streams the vocabulary in 8,192-wide chunks through a fragment and accumulates into a replicated reducer, with ties at exactly the sampled logprob resolved by column index so the result is deterministic; a negative `sample_results` entry (a rejected token) short-circuits the output to 0.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory for the tail-mass reduction; `vocab_size` fixes the chunk width at compile time and the kernel accumulates exp(logprob) over all entries ordered at or below the sampled token, emitting 0 for tokens marked rejected.

nodes.s: CUDA TileLang kernel expanding the four-column SWA pivot table — two (offset, length) pairs per row describing a window that may wrap the ring buffer — into a dense `n x width` index tensor: columns below `len1` map into the first segment, the next `len2` into the wrapped second segment, and the remainder are filled with -1 as padding. A small, purely index-generating kernel tiled four rows by up to 1,024 columns.

k.s: TileLang JIT factory for the SWA pivot expansion kernel; `width` is a compile-time constant setting the column tile, and the generated kernel materializes the two-segment wrapped window as explicit indices with -1 padding.

layers.name: Control Plane & Engine Core
layers.desc: The vLLM-derived request lifecycle and the only plane DeepInfer kept from vLLM: LLMEngine, the LLM entrypoint, CLI/arg parsing, EngineConfig, and the Sequence / SamplingParams data model. Also holds shm_broadcast, which fans the scheduler's decisions out to workers over shared memory, the stats logger and profile server, and the package-wide foundation utilities (logger, environment flags, attrdict, dynamic class loading, model-config resolution, timers). It admits requests, owns configuration, and hands batches down to the C++ scheduler.

layers.name: C++ Scheduling Core (csrc)
layers.desc: DeepSeek's from-scratch C++ hot path under csrc/, bound into Python with pybind11 and typed by the deepinfer/_C/*.pyi stubs. Despite sitting next to the kernels, this is CPU code: the 1,329-line batch Scheduler (it releases the GIL and runs a c10d allreduce across the DP group so every rank agrees on the same batch), the ref-counted KV block manager, the FLOPs estimator, ZOS zero-overhead-scheduling step remapping, MTP varlen sizing, and host-side preparation of input and sampling tensors. A WITH_NPU compile switch picks the CUDA or ACL device-memory and IPC backend, so the same scheduler compiles for both vendors.

layers.name: Model Execution Runtime
layers.desc: Per-rank forward-step machinery. The Worker / ModelRunner pair drives execution; CacheEngine owns KV-cache tensors; the CUDA-graph runners capture and replay decode steps, including the dFlash speculative-decoding variant, backed by a decode perf cache and ZOS status plumbing. The layer also holds the torch-module primitives the model is built from (FP8/DeepGEMM linear, layernorm, rotary embedding, vocab-parallel embedding, sampler, attention-backend selection), the GPU-side input-metadata builders for dFlash and YOCO, and the XGrammar structured-output subsystem, which lands here because its only consumer is the sampler that applies its logit masks.

layers.name: Model Definition & Checkpoint Loading
layers.desc: The DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash network itself. v4_modules/ supplies MLA attention, sparse index attention, KV compression, MoE and dense MLP, Engram memory, multi-way hyper-connections, the YOCO cross-layer cache and MTP heads; decoder_layer.py and deepseek.py assemble them, deepseek_vl.py wraps the vision-language variant, and mtp/ holds the draft model. hugging_face/ belongs in the same layer because it exists to fill these parameter containers: safetensors loading, checkpoint-to-module name mapping, FP8 scale handling, tokenizer and processor construction, and expert-parallel-aware weight sharding.

layers.name: TileLang Op Interface
layers.desc: The backend-neutral Python API for every TileLang kernel, and the surface the rest of the engine actually imports: 46 import edges arrive here from attention, KV compression, the cache engine, the sampler, input metadata and structured output. Each module exposes one typed entry point, resolves the physical KV-cache format (cache_common.py is the single source of truth for the five supported layouts), and calls ops.xxx_tl. ops.py is a 32-line dispatcher that pkgutil-discovers whichever backend package PLATFORM.tilelang_ops_backend names and re-exports its *_tl factories. Every module also carries its own pytest differential test against a torch reference in the same file, so each kernel's contract and its proof ship together.

layers.name: CUDA / SM100 Kernel Backend
layers.desc: The NVIDIA half of the execution layer: 29 TileLang kernel modules behind a deliberately empty package marker, discovered at import time by ops.py. Covers paged KV-cache load/store with FP8/FP4/MXFP8 quantization, fused transforms, RMSNorm with fused FP8 cast emitting the scale layouts DeepGEMM wants, sparse-attention candidate-block selection, FlashMLA helpers, speculative decoding (dFlash, MTP varlen scheduling, ZOS gathers), sampling and structured-output masking. Three modules exist only here — quant, outlier_detection and prepare_decode_metadata. It never imports the Ascend backend; the two are peers chosen at runtime.

layers.name: Ascend 950 Kernel Backend
layers.desc: The Huawei Ascend mirror of the CUDA backend, written kernel-for-kernel against CANN and torch-npu: the same 29-module surface, minus the three CUDA-only modules and plus three of its own (kv_quant, rstd_1ulp, prepare_v4_decode_metadata). Not a single import crosses between this layer and the CUDA backend — ops.py binds exactly one of them per process, which is what lets one engine build serve both vendors. Keeping it a separate layer makes the real cost visible: every new kernel has to be written twice.

layers.name: Parallelism & Expert Balancing
layers.desc: Process-group construction and collectives for the axes this engine actually uses — data, context, expert, expert-in-data, Engram and world. Notably there is no tensor-parallel axis anywhere in the repo. parallel_state.py is the group registry, reached by 21 modules across the engine, worker, model and metadata layers; alongside it sit context-parallel ring communication, NCCL memory accounting, user-buffer allocation, and the EPLB expert-placement policy with its live expert shuffle.

layers.name: Platform Abstraction & Hardware Discovery
layers.desc: The vendor switch that the rest of the tree reads but rarely branches on. platform.py resolves the active backend and names the TileLang backend package; npu_ops/ installs import hooks and monkey-patches that swap Ascend implementations in for CUDA-only ops such as DeepSelect and ViT attention, which is why it has no static import edges at all; deep_cluster/ enumerates NVIDIA and Ascend devices behind a single facade and handles NUMA and CPU binding through ctypes.

layers.name: Multimodal / Vision Pipeline
layers.desc: The image path, from raw bytes to embeddings. ve/ runs image, text and multimodal processors in separate processes and ships tensors back over shared memory with a versioned schema, plus chunked-prefill-aware tensor preparation; models/vision_encoder/ holds the ViT, the MLP projector and the VL aligner; multimodal_tokens.py defines the placeholder-token contract that ties vision output to the text sequence. A tightly cohesive path — the vision encoder modules have exactly one consumer, deepseek_vl.py.

layers.name: Build, Tests & Benchmarks
layers.desc: Everything outside the shipped runtime. The pytest suite covers end-to-end offline inference and perplexity regressions against a golden baseline, sampler statistical tests, batch-invariance and determinism checks, CUDA sync guards, and distributed expert-shuffle and user-buffer tests. examples/ is a real benchmark harness with launcher, tracing, Pareto sweep drivers and a YOCO equivalence check. The build side carries the two-platform story: setup.py, build_vendor.sh for FlashMLA / DeepGEMM / DeepEP and CANN, stub generation, clang-format, and per-vendor requirement pins, next to the project docs.

tour.title: Start with what DeepSeek did NOT release
tour.desc: Read the README first, but read it for the negative space. DeepInfer is the engine that runs DeepSeek's production service, yet what ships here is explicitly an offline engine: the README names three things as 'required for a complete inference service (not included in this release)' - the KV cache system, VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation, and load balancing across data-parallel replicas. If you come from vLLM you will reflexively look for an OpenAI-compatible server, a KV connector and a router; none of them are here, and that absence is the single most important fact about this codebase. What is here is everything below those layers: attention DP with balanced CP, MoE EP plus EPLB, DSpark speculative decoding, SWA bounded replay, zero-overhead async scheduling, batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling - each gated by a DEEPINFER_* environment variable rather than a CLI flag, which tells you the configuration surface is tuned by operators, not end users. The Acknowledgments section closes the loop: 'DeepInfer was originally built primarily on vLLM, with additional inspiration from SGLang and TensorRT-LLM.' The rest of this tour is about how much of that vLLM origin survived, and where it was torn out.

tour.title: The vLLM lineage: a control plane that survived, a model layer that did not
tour.desc: Exactly 23 source files carry the header comment '# Derived from vLLM; modified by DeepSeek.' Where they sit is the whole story. Measured by lines of code, entrypoints/ and distributed/ are 100% derived, worker/ is 81%, engine/ is 58% - but model_executor/ is 4%. DeepSeek kept vLLM's request lifecycle skeleton and rewrote everything that touches a tensor. Open llm_engine.py and you will recognize the shape immediately: an LLMEngine that owns a scheduler, block manager and worker processes and drives a step() loop. Then look closer - the scheduler it owns is a C++ object, and DeferredRelease holds each step's sequence metadata and block unpins back by one iteration so recycling overlaps GPU work. model_runner.py is the same bargain at the worker level: the familiar driver-prepares-and-broadcasts / followers-receive pattern, wrapped around an input-metadata builder and CUDA-graph machinery that are entirely DeepSeek's. config.py is where the divergence is most legible - ModelConfig, CacheConfig, ParallelConfig and SchedulerConfig are all still there, but ParallelConfig has no tensor_parallel_size field at all. entrypoints/llm.py is vLLM's LLM convenience class, and it is the only entrypoint in the repo.

tour.title: The inversion: the scheduler went down into C++, the kernels went up into a DSL
tour.desc: This is the step that reframes the whole repo. csrc/engine/scheduler.hpp is 1,329 lines of C++ implementing continuous batching - waiting/running/prompted queues, prompt chunking that refuses to split an image, block allocation, preemption under KV pressure, and folding sampler results back into sequence state. It runs with py::gil_scoped_release held, so batch scheduling for the next step proceeds while Python is busy elsewhere. More interesting is how it stays consistent across data-parallel ranks: every rank must execute the same step shape (prefill or decode) or the collectives deadlock, so the scheduler does a c10d allreduce over the DP group and votes. The vote has two flavors deliberately - an ALL point every prefill_attempt_interval decode steps (everyone must want prefill), and an ANY point every prefill_any_attempt_interval steps (one rank wanting it is enough). The ANY round exists purely to stop a lone rank's prefill work from being starved forever by the ALL rule; the in-source comments spell out the livelock it prevents. Now the counterpart: search the repo for *.cu files and you get zero. Not one hand-written CUDA kernel. The hot path moved in both directions at once - scheduling down into C++, kernels up into a Python DSL. pybind_scheduler.cpp is the seam, and _C/engine.pyi is the authoritative inventory of what crossed over: 21 classes and 13 free functions, including the entire Sequence object model that lives in Python in vLLM.

tour.title: ZOS: what 'zero-overhead scheduling' actually costs to build
tour.desc: vLLM 1.x overlaps CPU scheduling with GPU execution too, so the idea will be familiar - but look at the plumbing DeepSeek needed to make it work with speculative decoding in the loop. The problem: to build step N+1's decode inputs on the CPU you need step N's sampled tokens, which are still on the GPU. ZOS refuses to wait. zos.cpp remaps the current step's sequences onto the previous step's slot order so GPU-resident state is reused verbatim, and builds padded seqlen / block-table / token tensors (including Engram n-gram rows) from stale CPU state. prepare_tensor_input_zos.py then has TileLang gather kernels splice the previous step's sampled and predicted tokens into those tensors on-device, and worker.py corrects the sequence lengths on-GPU after the fact, deferring the decode step's post-processing by one iteration. zos_status.py is the small dataclass pair that carries this across the step boundary: a worker output still awaiting post-processing, plus the remap and corrected seqlens. The payoff is that the CPU never blocks on the GPU; the price is that correctness now depends on a fixup pass, which is exactly why the repo has batch-invariance and determinism tests.

tour.title: One engine, two vendors: the platform switch
tour.desc: platform.py is small and worth reading line by line, because it is the hinge the entire two-vendor story turns on. A Platform base class declares exactly three things that differ: tilelang_ops_backend (the directory name 'cuda' or 'asc'), distributed_backend ('nccl' or 'hccl'), and fp8_sf_type (torch.int32 on NVIDIA, torch.int16 on Ascend - the FP8 scale-factor word size differs, and that propagates into every quantized cache layout). PlatformNPU's __init__ is where the pragmatism shows: it pins TILELANG_DEFAULT_TARGET because torch_npu's transfer_to_npu shim makes torch.cuda.is_available() return True on an NPU-only host, sets HCCL buffer sizes, and resolves aclrtHostRegisterV2 out of libascendcl.so by ctypes to get pinned host memory. deep_cluster/hardware/device.py is the layer underneath - device counts, physical ids, NUMA node, BF16 TFLOPS ceiling - behind one facade. And npu_ops/patch_imports.py is the escape hatch: it installs a builtins.__import__ hook that hands back lazy proxies, so Ascend implementations can be swapped in for CUDA-only ops like DeepSelect and ViT attention without a single static import edge. That is why npu_ops/ looks disconnected in any import graph of this repo.

tour.title: TileLang: 32 lines of dispatcher where vLLM has a C++ op registry
tour.desc: This is the largest subsystem in the repo and the one with no vLLM counterpart. ops.py is the entire dispatch mechanism - 32 lines. It imports the backend package named by PLATFORM.tilelang_ops_backend, walks it with pkgutil.iter_modules, and hoists every symbol ending in _tl into its own namespace, asserting on collisions. A module __getattr__ raises KernelUnavailableError for anything the selected backend lacks. That is it: no registry, no dispatch keys, no torch.library. cuda/__init__.py and asc/__init__.py are deliberately empty - declaring re-exports there would defeat the pkgutil walk. The ~30 top-level tilelang_ops/*.py modules are the backend-neutral interface: one typed entry point each, resolving the physical cache format and calling ops.xxx_tl. cache_common.py is the single source of truth for that format - a frozen KVCacheFormat dataclass covering five layouts (FP8/FP4 main cache, FP4/FP8/MXFP8 index caches) with derived byte strides, and the torch reference casts the tests compare against. Note what is absent: there is no GEMM kernel anywhere in tilelang_ops. Dense math is delegated wholesale to DeepGEMM, FlashMLA and TileKernels. 29 of the 33 top-level modules import pytest, because each kernel ships its differential test against a torch reference in the same file; conftest.py binds each xdist worker to its own GPU and turns KernelUnavailableError into a skip.

tour.title: One kernel, written twice - the real price of the two-backend design
tour.desc: Read these three files together and the cost model becomes concrete. store_kv_cache.py is the neutral interface: infer the cache format, skip -1 padding slots, quantize on the way in. Its torch reference path already carries two Ascend-specific workarounds (torch_npu's IndexPutV2 32-bit offset wraparound, and slot-0 padding aliasing) - the abstraction leaks even before you reach a backend. cuda/store_kv_cache.py specializes by logical layout and emits ue8m0 scales into paged slots. asc/store_kv_cache.py solves the same problem with a completely different strategy: quantize in registers into one aligned UB row, then one exact-length DMA per row or run. Same contract, nothing shared. Not a single import crosses between the cuda/ and asc/ packages - they are peers, and ops.py binds exactly one per process. The asymmetry is small but real: three modules exist only on CUDA (quant, outlier_detection, prepare_decode_metadata) and three only on Ascend (kv_quant, rstd_1ulp, prepare_v4_decode_metadata). If you have ever argued about whether to support a second accelerator, this is the ledger: every new kernel is written twice, and the differential test in the neutral module is what keeps the two honest.

tour.title: Parallelism with no tensor-parallel axis, and experts rebalanced at runtime
tour.desc: Grep the source tree for 'tensor parallel' in any spelling and you get zero hits. For a reader whose mental model of large-model serving starts with TP=8, this is the sharpest break from vLLM in the repo. parallel_state.py is the group registry - 21 modules across the engine, worker, model and metadata layers reach into it - and the axes it builds are data (dp), context (cp), expert (ep and ep_in_dp), engram (enp), world and local, plus gloo CPU mirrors and a shared-memory MessageQueue on the CP group for object broadcast; the rank layouts are derived with einops rearrange over a single 1-D rank tensor, so each axis is literally a reshape of the global rank order. The consequence shows up in linear.py: the only linear layer in the engine is replicated, never sharded, and the GEMM itself is handed to DeepGEMM (bf16_gemm_nt / fp8_fp4_gemm_nt) - the module's own job is output-buffer allocation at 32-byte alignment and the FP8 cast recipe. Attention is replicated per DP rank; the model is split by experts, not by hidden dimension. Which makes expert load imbalance, not activation sharding, the thing that decides decode throughput - so placement is runtime state here, not a startup decision. eplb/policy.py is a batched greedy assignment that spreads each logical expert's measured token load across its physical replicas, and eplb/shuffle.py actually moves the weights mid-run: a general NCCL batched-P2P path plus a single-node fast path that reads peer weights through symmetric-memory / IPC mirrors, both rewriting weight tensors in place.

tour.title: Engram: a parallel axis that exists for one layer type
tour.desc: Engram is the piece of DeepSeek-V4.1 with no analogue in any model vLLM serves, and it earned its own entry in parallel_state's axis list (enp). It is a hash-indexed n-gram memory: engram_metadata.py builds a normalized original-to-compressed token mapping on CPU, derives a static per-layer/per-head table layout from distinct primes, and materializes the hash multipliers, vocab sizes and offsets the kernels consume - with a warning that table identity depends on the exact NumPy RNG seed, so changing it shifts every hashed table id. engram.py is the runtime: it maps raw tokens onto the compressed vocabulary, fetches the rank-sharded embedding tables through DeepEP's EngramBuffer, projects them with a fused KV projection, and gates the result into the hidden states with a fused TileKernels op. The engineering detail worth stealing: the tables live in a DeepEP userbuffer written once at startup, and the per-step fetch returns one lazy hook per Engram layer, so the cross-rank gather overlaps with the layers that run before it. engram_parameters.py holds the rank-local slice, row-padded to the LCM of 256 and the Engram parallel size. Read this as a worked example of adding a new sharded memory to an engine: a parallel group, a collective buffer, a loader path, and a lazily-awaited gather.

tour.title: Attention: MLA, a sparse indexer, and YOCO's truncated prefill
tour.desc: attn.py is the largest file in the model layer, and it carries three mechanisms that are usually three separate features elsewhere. First, MLA: Q/KV projection and fusion, compressed-KV storage, with mla_attn.py holding the low-rank Wq/Wkv containers. compress.py runs the gated low-rank KV compression plus RMSNorm and stores the post-RoPE value into the paged cache through a single fused norm/RoPE/Hadamard/cast/store kernel - the pre-RoPE latent it returns is what feeds the indexer. Second, sparse attention: index_attn.py is an MQA indexer that computes relu(q@k)*weights logits against an FP4 index-KV cache and selects the top-k compressed KV blocks per query, with separate prefill and decode metadata paths. So there are two KV caches here, a main one and a much smaller FP4 index one, which is why cache_common.py needed five layouts. Third, YOCO: yoco.py decides which layers are consumers and compacts hidden states, HC lazy data and cross-layer index caches at the truncation boundary (gathering across CP ranks when CP is on). That is the 'SWA bounded replay' the README advertises - on reprefill you replay only a bounded suffix instead of the whole prompt, which is a cache-miss recovery strategy, not a model feature.

tour.title: mHC and the assembled model: the residual stream is not a single vector
tour.desc: Multi-way hyper-connections replace the plain residual stream, and they change the shape of the thing flowing through the network - worth knowing before you read any forward pass here. hc.py's HCLayerMixin expands the residual into an hc_mult-way trunk, mixes it into each sub-layer input (pre) and folds the sub-layer output back (post), with a single-call deep_gemm.mega_mhc fusion on GPU; HCHead collapses the trunk back to one hidden state before the LM head. hc_lazy.py is a deliberately import-free dataclass that carries the trunk and its mixing coefficients from _hc_pre to the paired hc_post, so a post and the next pre can be fused into one kernel - and so the YOCO operator layer can inspect and rebuild it without pulling in the fused kernel stack. decoder_layer.py chains it all: HC attention-norm with Engram injected as a post-HC trunk hook, V4 attention, FFN norm, MoE MLP, plus the YOCO compaction boundary. deepseek.py is the assembly point - embedding, layer stack, Engram runtime, YOCO boundary, LM head, sampler, DFlash MTP, EPLB groups, userbuffer, and checkpoint loading end to end. Note where context parallelism lives: hidden states are gathered into the CP zigzag mirror layout before the layer loop and all-gathered back after, entirely at the model boundary.

tour.title: DSpark: speculative decoding that schedules itself
tour.desc: vLLM's spec-decode gives every request the same draft length. DeepInfer does not, and mtp_varlen.hpp is where that decision is made - in C++, from measurements. It tracks median sampler and forward-step runtimes, picks the throughput-optimal total query count against a measured (batch_size, forward_ms) curve, and then hands each request its own seqlen_q by sorting draft tokens on predicted accept rate. That is the 'confidence-scheduled verification' the README names: requests whose drafts look likely to be accepted get more verification budget, and the batch width is chosen to sit at the knee of the measured latency curve rather than at a configured constant. dflash.py is the draft model itself - a confidence head that scores each draft token, plus a driver that writes main-token keys from captured target-layer features and runs the draft layers over a fixed-stride window. input_metadata/dflash.py builds that fixed-stride draft layout with one fused TileLang launch specifically so it can be captured in a CUDA graph, and dflash_cuda_graph_runner.py captures the draft decode on the same batch-size ladder as the main graph. Two graph ladders, one per model, replayed in lockstep.

tour.title: Weight loading: no vLLM lineage, and it shows
tour.desc: hugging_face/ is DeepSeek-original code with no vLLM ancestry, and it is stricter than what you are used to. loading.py is a validation front end that runs before a single weight byte is read: it proves every shard named by model.safetensors.index.json exists and is readable, builds HFCoverage groups, resolves MTP tied-parameter aliases, and rejects shape or dtype mismatches straight from the safetensors headers. names.py is a pure mapping table from HF tensor names to internal module.module.{i}. paths, covering embeddings, backbone, head, MTP layers, the vision tower and Engram tensors - a single flat place to look when a checkpoint will not load. weights.py does the real work through three distinct channels, which tells you how heterogeneous this model's parameters are: per-parameter loading (with the w1/w3 dim-0 merge), layer-aggregated routed experts written directly in the runtime 3D packed FP4 layout, and row-chunked Engram n-gram tables. parameters.py defines what the loader may write into and packs UE8M0 FP8 scale factors via TileKernels batched_transpose_weight_sf, explicitly refusing MXFP4 expert and Engram parameters because those own dedicated packing paths. The pattern to take away: quantized and sharded formats are materialized at load time, not converted at runtime.

tour.title: Multimodal and structured output: two subsystems that shape the token stream
tour.desc: The vision path (ve/, for Vision Encoder) is built as a separable service, which is consistent with the README's note that VE/prefill/decode disaggregation is 'most required engine functionality already implemented' but not shipped. multimodal_processor.py runs HF preprocessing in forked worker processes, rewrites prompts to expand the image placeholder token, writes image tensors into a shared pinned pool, and handles hang detection and aborts. schema.py owns the shared-pool handle lifecycle with two distinct free paths - immediate on abort, deferred and event-gated on normal prefill - which is the kind of detail that only exists after a production leak. multimodal_tokens.py is the single source of truth for image special-token ids and the mm_token_type wire format shared by the VE processors, the MoE gate (remember the separate image routing bias) and the embedding-replacement kernel. deepseek_vl.py stacks the ViT and aligner on the causal LM and fuses image embeddings into token embeddings before the stack runs. Structured output lands next to the sampler because that is its only consumer: matcher.py wraps an xgrammar GrammarMatcher that stays dormant until a KMP-matched trigger sequence fires, supports MTP-depth rollback (drafts can be rejected, so the grammar state must rewind), and sampler.py applies the resulting bitmask alongside blacklist and EOS masks - vLLM's per-request Python sampling loop is gone, replaced by packed total_q tensors handed to TileLang kernels.

tour.title: Run it, measure it, then read what production actually looks like
tour.desc: Finish where you would start if you were bringing this up. offline_inference.py is the reference script - EP/DP/CP sizes, a fixed prompt set, and per-sample output with token counts, speculative acceptance rate and decode perplexity; on NVIDIA it defaults DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 so those PPLs are bit-reproducible and serve as a golden baseline, and its print format is parsed by a test and must not change. benchmark.py is a serious harness: it derives the parallel topology from visible devices, builds synthetic text or image workloads at a given context length and cached-prefix ratio, and runs prefill and decode as separate steady-state measurement windows with warmup steps, burned steps around the profiler windows, forced load balance and a pinned MoE flush interval - every one of those is a defense against a number you would otherwise misread. examples/README.md explains exactly which intervals are discarded and how the three reported metrics are computed. Then read doc/inference_deployment_qa.md last, because it describes the system this release is a component of: sixteen sections on the disaggregated E/P/D topology and its parallelism choices (EP2-8/DP2-8 for prefill, EP64-128 Wide-EP for decode, and explicitly no TP and no CP in production), the dedicated 3FS KV-cache cluster with its erasure coding and TTLs, EPLB and DP load balancing, SWA bounded replay's hit/recompute policy, where FP4 is used, which kernel library backs which operation, and measured DSpark gains. That document is the missing half of the README's exclusion list.
